summary: 18 claims on whether prediction, early warning and data-driven planning save lives and money, each checked against a fetched page, PDF or paper record. Lives: Ahmedabad's heat action plan (1,190 deaths avoided a year, wide range), Philadelphia (117 lives for about $210,000) and France in 2006 (about 4,400 fewer deaths than expected). Money: early warning returns at least ten times its cost (Global Commission on Adaptation), a Madrid benefit to cost range of 12 to 3700, and a plantation programme with a 22 percent return. Gulf: Qatar's WBGT stop-work rule came with clinic visits down by more than half, and Saudi rules scale breaks by Heat Index and ask employers to measure temperature and humidity. Prediction: a Saudi construction model scores incident severity at 83 to 89 percent accuracy using weather inputs, lightning warnings reach 20 to 72 minutes of lead time, and heat stress forecasts are skilful out to 10 days. All of these are external published results. None measures a WakeCap system.

claims.topic: Ahmedabad Heat Action Plan: deaths avoided per year
claims.figure: An estimated 1,190 (95% CI 162 to 2,218) average annualized deaths avoided after the plan began; the peak heat risk ratio fell from 2.34 to 1.25 at 47 C
claims.measures: Status: stat (observational pilot evaluation). All-cause deaths in 2014 to 2015 after the plan, compared with a 2007 to 2010 baseline. The plan is South Asia's first heat action plan: warnings, public advisories and health-sector preparedness. The range is wide, and the post-to-pre incidence rate ratio for days above 40 C was 0.95 (0.73 to 1.22), so treat 1,190 as an estimate and not as proof.
claims.year: 2014-2015 after the plan, against a 2007-2010 baseline; published 2018
claims.source_title: Building Resilience to Climate Change: Pilot Evaluation of the Impact of India's First Heat Action Plan on All-Cause Mortality
claims.publisher: Journal of Environmental and Public Health (full text on PubMed Central, PMC6236972)
claims.quote: An estimated 1,190 (95%CI 162–2,218) average annualized deaths were avoided in the post-HAP period.
claims.use_in_story: Count a city skyline up to 1,190 lives a year and show the wide uncertainty range as a soft glow so the claim stays honest.

claims.topic: Philadelphia heat warning system: lives saved against cost
claims.figure: 117 lives saved in three years (1995 to 1998), about 2.6 lives per warning day; system cost about $210,000; gross benefit about $468 million
claims.measures: Status: stat (modelled estimate). Compares daily deaths with and without a Hot Weather-Health Watch/Warning System warning. The benefit uses a $4 million value of a life (117 x $4 million). The cost counts about $10,000 per warning day over 21 warning days. The paper says the lives saved could be 20% to 50% lower once deaths that were only brought forward in time are removed. Bulletin of the AMS 85(8), PDF pages: abstract line p.1067, 2.6 lives p.1069, cost and $468 million p.1070, displacement note p.1071. DOI 10.1175/BAMS-85-8-1067.
claims.source_title: Heat Watch/Warning Systems Save Lives: Estimated Costs and Benefits for Philadelphia 1995-98
claims.publisher: Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society (copy hosted by the University of Delaware)
claims.quote: gross benefits of the Philadelphia heat wave warning system could be on the order of $468 million (117 lives saved times $4 million)
claims.use_in_story: Stack a $210,000 coin pile next to 117 lives and a $468 million bar so the cost of a warning looks tiny.

claims.topic: France 2006 heat wave: deaths against the 2003 baseline
claims.figure: About 2065 excess deaths in the July 2006 heat wave against 6452 predicted if 2003 vulnerability had stayed; approximately 4400 fewer deaths
claims.measures: Status: stat (modelled counterfactual). Excess deaths from 11 to 28 July 2006, compared with a model built on 1975 to 2003 temperature and death data. France set up a warning system and prevention measures after 2003. The authors read the gap as lower vulnerability, more awareness, preventive measures and the warning system together, not the warning alone. DOI link: https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dym253 (International Journal of Epidemiology 37(2), abstract read from the Europe PMC record).
claims.source_title: Has the impact of heat waves on mortality changed in France since the European heat wave of summer 2003? A study of the 2006 heat wave
claims.publisher: International Journal of Epidemiology (abstract via Europe PMC)
claims.quote: The observed mortality during the 2006 heat wave was thus markedly less than the expected mortality (approximately 4400 less deaths).
claims.use_in_story: Draw two bars for the same heat wave, 6,452 deaths expected and about 2,065 seen, and let the 4,400 gap pulse.

claims.topic: Early warning: 24 hours of notice, damage avoided and return on cost
claims.figure: 24 hours warning of a storm or heat wave cuts the damage by 30 percent; early warning systems save lives and assets worth at least ten times their cost; $800 million of such systems in developing countries would avoid $3 to 16 billion of losses per year
claims.measures: Status: stat (commission estimate, all hazards, not workplace specific). Printed in Box ES.1 (page labelled 5) and in Chapter 1 (page labelled 14) of the report. WMO repeats the 30 percent and $3 to 16 billion figures in a news item of 21 March 2022 (https://wmo.int/news/media-centre/early-warning-systems-must-protect-everyone-within-five-years). WMO's Early Warnings for All page (https://wmo.int/activities/early-warnings-all, shown as updated 27 July 2026) says early warning 'provides a nearly tenfold return on investment'.
claims.region: Global (developing countries for the $800 million case)
claims.source_title: Adapt Now: A Global Call for Leadership on Climate Resilience
claims.quote: Just 24 hours warning of a coming storm or heat wave can cut the ensuing damage by 30 percent
claims.use_in_story: Tick a 24 hour clock down before a heat wave while a damage bar drops 30 percent, then flash the ten times return.

claims.topic: Heat warning system economics: benefit to cost ratio for Madrid
claims.figure: Benefit-cost ratio from 12 to 3700 for a heat warning system in Madrid, depending on how a death is valued
claims.measures: Status: stat (modelled estimate). Three valuation schemes: value of a statistical life for all deaths, a mixed scheme, and a conservative value of a life year scheme. The lowest ratio comes from the conservative scheme. The authors warn that in other places the conservative scheme could give ratios well below 1. Show it as a range and never as one number. DOI link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11027-017-9778-4 (Mitigation and Adaptation Strategies for Global Change; full text on PubMed Central as PMC6105260).
claims.source_title: Valuing deaths or years of life lost? Economic benefits of avoided mortality from early heat warning systems
claims.publisher: Mitigation and Adaptation Strategies for Global Change (abstract via Europe PMC)
claims.quote: When applying these three schemes to Madrid (Spain), we obtain a benefit-cost ratio varying from 12 to 3700.
claims.use_in_story: Slide a benefit to cost balance from 12 to 1 up to 3,700 to 1 and label the low end as the cautious case.

claims.topic: Qatar WBGT stop-work rule and heat illness visits
claims.figure: Heat-related hospitalizations in Qatar fell by more than half after the 2021 rule (outdoor work banned 10:00 to 15:30 from 1 June to 15 September, and all work stops above 32.1 C WBGT)
claims.measures: Status: stat (observational before and after, one summer). ILO reports Qatar Red Crescent clinic data for the first summer under Ministerial Decision No. 17 of 2021, compared with 2019 and 2020. The report shows a chart and the text says 'more than half', so there is no exact count. The rule has a measured heat trigger (WBGT 32.1 C) as well as fixed hours. ILO report PDF page 50 (printed page 36), citing an earlier ILO 2021 report that was not fetched. Canonical ILO page: https://www.ilo.org/publications/heat-work-implications-safety-and-health.
claims.year: Summer 2021 against 2019 and 2020; ILO review published 25 July 2024
claims.source_title: Heat at work: Implications for safety and health
claims.quote: hospitalizations associated with workplace heat stress in Qatar were reduced by more than half after adoption of Ministerial Decision No.17
claims.use_in_story: Draw a work-stop line at WBGT 32.1 C, then drop the clinic visit bars to under half to show what a measured trigger can do.

claims.topic: Saudi heat rules: break share by Heat Index and a duty to measure on site
claims.figure: Heat Index 30 to 38 C: 25% of work time on breaks; 39 to 51 C: 50%; 52 C or more: 75%; work suspended at 56 C or more; employers must provide temperature and humidity measuring devices
claims.measures: Status: stat (regulation as summarised by ILO). Described for Ministerial Decree No. 3337, in force 15 June to 15 September each year with a 12:00 to 15:00 outdoor work ban. Low risk is 25 to 29 C. The ministry's own guide was not fetched, so the thresholds are as printed by ILO. ILO report PDF page 51 (printed page 37).
claims.year: Rule in force each summer; ILO review published 25 July 2024
claims.source_title: Heat at work: Implications for safety and health
claims.quote: Work should be suspended when the Heat Index reaches 56°C or more. ... employers must provide temperature- and humidity-measuring devices
claims.use_in_story: Show a Heat Index ladder with 25, 50 and 75 percent break bars and a chip for the on-site thermometer and hygrometer the rule asks for.

claims.topic: Sugar plantation heat programme: kidney injury, productivity and return
claims.figure: Acute kidney injury cases down 94 percent; fatal heatstroke eliminated; productivity up 10 to 20 percent; 22 percent positive return on investment, in the first three years
claims.measures: Status: stat (programme-reported results summarised by ILO). The plan was mandated breaks through the year, mobile shade tents, purified water with an electrolyte drink and field sanitation, on a 75,000 hectare plantation. ILO report PDF page 85 (printed page 71). The underlying studies were not fetched, and the results come from the programme partners.
claims.year: First three years of the programme; ILO review published 25 July 2024
claims.source_title: Heat at work: Implications for safety and health (Adelante Initiative case study)
claims.quote: increased productivity by 10-20 per cent and provided a 22 per cent positive return on investment as accidents, staff turnover and absenteeism were reduced
claims.use_in_story: Pop three counters together: kidney injury minus 94 percent, productivity plus 10 to 20 percent, return 22 percent.

claims.topic: Acclimatization: when heat deaths happen in a new job
claims.figure: Over 70 percent of heat-related deaths occur in a worker's first week; almost half occur on the first day on the job or the first day back after a long absence
claims.measures: Status: stat. OSHA page for new workers. It cites a 2018 OSHA case series that was not fetched. A separate review of 2012 to 2013 OSHA enforcement cases (MMWR, PMC4584656, fetched) found 13 worker deaths, nine in the first 3 days and four on day one. OSHA's rule of thumb is 20 percent of normal work on day one, then 20 percent more each day.
claims.publisher: US Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
claims.quote: Over 70 percent of heat-related deaths occur during a worker's first week
claims.use_in_story: Light up a seven day strip where most of the danger sits in days one to seven, and tie it to a new-worker flag on the permit.

claims.topic: A site WBGT limit catches deaths that a Heat Index alert can miss
claims.figure: WBGT-based exposure limits were exceeded in all 14 fatal cases and in 8 of 11 non-fatal cases; 6 fatalities occurred when the Heat Index was below 91 F (32.8 C); 11 of 14 deaths (78.6%) were unacclimatized workers
claims.measures: Status: stat (case review, small sample). 25 outdoor heat illnesses (14 fatal, 11 non-fatal) investigated by OSHA from 2011 to 2016. The Heat Index and acclimatization figures are in the same summary box and table. It shows why a site-level WBGT and a worker's acclimatization status matter, not only a regional Heat Index.
claims.source_title: Evaluation of Occupational Exposure Limits for Heat Stress in Outdoor Workers - United States, 2011-2016
claims.publisher: CDC Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (full text on PubMed Central, PMC6048976)
claims.quote: WBGT-based occupational exposure limits were exceeded for all 14 fatalities and for eight of 11 nonfatal illnesses.
claims.use_in_story: Show a regional Heat Index dial stuck on green while a site WBGT dial passes its limit, one dot per case.

claims.topic: Wearable heat strain: core temperature estimated from heart rate
claims.figure: Core temperature estimate from heart rate has a bias of -0.03 C (spread 0.32 C); 95% of estimates fall within 0.63 C of the measured value, over more than 52,000 observations
claims.measures: Status: stat (peer-reviewed validation, no injury outcome). A Kalman filter model trained on 17 volunteers in a 24 hour military field exercise and checked on 83 laboratory and field subjects across heat, hydration, clothing and acclimation states. The authors say it does not replace direct measurement (esophageal against rectal limits of agreement average 0.58 C) but is accurate enough as a practical work-strain indicator. DOI link: https://doi.org/10.1088/0967-3334/34/7/781 (Physiological Measurement, abstract read from the Europe PMC record).
claims.region: Not stated in the abstract (military field exercise and laboratory studies)
claims.source_title: Estimation of human core temperature from sequential heart rate observations
claims.quote: overall bias of -0.03 ± 0.32 °C and that 95% of all CT estimates fall within ±0.63 °C
claims.use_in_story: Draw a worker's heart rate line turning into a core temperature curve with a thin plus or minus 0.63 C band.

claims.topic: Saudi construction incidents: a model predicts severity, with weather as inputs
claims.figure: XGBoost predicted incident severity (scale 1 to 5) with 83% accuracy from 14 project, worker and weather variables, and 89% when the nature of the incident was added; 82% for the nature of the incident
claims.measures: Status: stat (peer-reviewed model on small data). 203 recorded incidents from 2018 to 2024, mostly Makkah and Riyadh, with an 80/20 train-test split. The 14 inputs include temperature, wind speed and precipitation. Without the nature of incident as an input, precipitation had the top feature importance for severity (about 0.30), and the paper's SHAP analysis names nature of incident, precipitation and date of incident as the most influential features. The authors say the small sample and two regions may limit generalisation. DOI link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-34763-0 (Scientific Reports, 10 January 2026).
claims.source_title: Machine learning applications for predicting safety incidents in construction industry
claims.publisher: Scientific Reports (full text on PubMed Central, PMC12867970)
claims.quote: XGB remained the most effective model, achieving an accuracy of 89% when using X1-X14 and NOI as input variables
claims.use_in_story: Show incident cards flowing into a model that scores severity 1 to 5, with temperature, wind and rain chips lighting up as inputs.

claims.topic: Construction site risk forecast from inspection data (Singapore)
claims.figure: A random forest classified site safety risk with accuracy 0.78 and weighted kappa 0.70 (substantial agreement)
claims.measures: Status: stat (peer-reviewed model). Data from one large contractor, 2010 to 2016: safety inspection records, accident cases and project data. 13 of 33 input variables were kept and five algorithms were tested. The authors recommend a monthly forecast of project safety performance so inspections can be targeted. DOI link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.autcon.2018.03.022 (Automation in Construction, abstract read from the Semantic Scholar record).
claims.source_title: Safety leading indicators for construction sites: A machine learning approach
claims.publisher: Automation in Construction (abstract via Semantic Scholar)
claims.quote: an accuracy of 0.78 and has achieved a substantial strength of agreement with Weighted-Kappa Statistics of 0.70
claims.use_in_story: Colour a portfolio of sites from green to red by predicted risk and show a monthly refresh that sends inspectors to the red ones first.

claims.topic: Singapore construction site pilot: scheduled breaks, cold water, cooler clothing
claims.figure: On the plan day workers clocked 10 percent more steps and a 14 percent higher step rate than on a normal day
claims.measures: Status: stat (one-site pilot, two monitored days). One outdoor construction site in May 2023. Workers were monitored on a normal day, then a week later on a day with heat education, three extra 15 minute shaded breaks, cold water and cooler work clothing. Heat strain and self-reported strain were similar on both days, and ILO calls the step gain 'a possible increase in productivity'. ILO report PDF page 86 (printed page 72).
claims.source_title: Heat at work: Implications for safety and health (HeatSafe project case study)
claims.quote: on the intervention day workers clocked a 10 per cent higher step count and a 14 per cent higher step rate
claims.use_in_story: Show two walking trails on a site map, a normal day and a plan day, with the plan day trail 10 percent longer.

claims.topic: Lightning warning from one weather station's basic readings
claims.figure: A machine learning model using 4 surface readings (air pressure, air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed) from one site had predictive skill for lead times up to 30 minutes
claims.measures: Status: stat (peer-reviewed model). Warnings were checked against lightning location systems and beat three baselines: persistence, a ground electric-field threshold and a CAPE threshold. The abstract gives no hit rate or false alarm rate and does not name the region. The publisher page was behind a cookie redirect, so only the abstract was read. DOI link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41612-019-0098-0 (npj Climate and Atmospheric Science, volume 2, article 41).
claims.source_title: Nowcasting lightning occurrence from commonly available meteorological parameters using machine learning techniques
claims.publisher: npj Climate and Atmospheric Science (abstract via Crossref)
claims.quote: the model has statistically considerable predictive skill for lead times up to 30 min
claims.use_in_story: Animate four small station dials (pressure, temperature, humidity, wind) feeding a lightning clock that reaches 30 minutes ahead.

claims.topic: Lightning rate jumps give minutes of warning before severe weather
claims.figure: Average lead time 20.65 minutes with total lightning against 13.54 minutes with cloud-to-ground only; probability of detection 79% against 66%; false alarm rate 36% against 53%; 711 thunderstorms
claims.measures: Status: stat (peer-reviewed verification). A rule that flags a sudden rise in total lightning rate, tested on 711 storms in four US regions. The lead time is before severe weather at the ground, not before a strike at a site. DOI link: https://doi.org/10.1175/WAF-D-10-05026.1 (Weather and Forecasting 26(5), abstract read from the Crossref record).
claims.source_title: Lightning and Severe Weather: A Comparison between Total and Cloud-to-Ground Lightning Trends
claims.publisher: Weather and Forecasting, American Meteorological Society (abstract via Crossref)
claims.quote: average lead times prior to severe weather occurrence were higher using total lightning as compared with CG lightning (20.65 versus 13.54 min)
claims.use_in_story: Draw a storm cell with a flash-rate spike and a 20 minute lead bar, with 79 percent of severe events caught and 36 percent of alerts false.

claims.topic: Lightning jump plus radar tracking: lead time for 1 hour and 2 hour forecasts
claims.figure: Lead time 47.8 minutes for 1-hour forecasts and 71.6 minutes for 2-hour forecasts; for 2-hour forecasts probability of detection 73.2% and false alarm rate 42.4% in 2024
claims.measures: Status: stat (peer-reviewed operational test). Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei, 2023 to 2024: lightning jump detection joined with radar storm tracking and extrapolation, for hail, gales and heavy rain. The warnings target severe convective weather, not strikes at a site. DOI link: https://doi.org/10.1155/adme/4280862 (Advances in Meteorology, abstract read from the Crossref record).
claims.source_title: An Operational and Real-Time Severe Weather Nowcasting System Based on Lightning Jumps: Introduction and Evaluation
claims.quote: The lead time increased to 47.8 min (+3.7%) for the 1-h forecasts and 71.6 min (+6.1%) for the 2-h forecasts.
claims.use_in_story: Show a 1 hour and a 2 hour arrow leaving a storm tracker, with lead bars of 47.8 and 71.6 minutes.

claims.topic: Heat stress forecast skill (UTCI) out to 10 days
claims.figure: Global probabilistic forecasts of the Universal Thermal Climate Index are skilful for lead times up to 10 days
claims.measures: Status: stat (peer-reviewed verification). Probabilistic forecasts beat single deterministic forecasts and were shown on the 2010 Russian heat wave. This is a skill result and not a percent accuracy, and skill varies by region. DOI link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s00484-014-0843-3 (International Journal of Biometeorology, abstract read from the Semantic Scholar record).
claims.source_title: Global forecasting of thermal health hazards: the skill of probabilistic predictions of the Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI)
claims.publisher: International Journal of Biometeorology (abstract via Semantic Scholar)
claims.quote: despite global variations, the UTCI forecast is skilful for lead times up to 10 days
claims.use_in_story: Show a 10 day forecast fan that widens each day, with a marker on day 10 where the skill ends.

gaps: The WebSearch budget (200 of 200 calls) ran out part way through. Topics found late (wearables, heat forecast skill, workplace programmes) were reached by fetching known papers and report PDFs. No further discovery was possible after that.

No heat forecast accuracy figure from a national weather service was fetched, for example the share of days with a maximum temperature within 2 C. The only heat forecast skill number is the UTCI result (skilful up to 10 days, global). The Met Office page only says its four-day forecast is as accurate as its one-day forecast was 30 years ago.

No peer-reviewed lives-saved study for a heat early-warning system in Saudi Arabia or another Gulf state was found. Qatar's drop in clinic visits is a before and after comparison for one summer. The Saudi rule is a fixed calendar ban plus a Heat Index scale, not a forecast.
The Saudi Heat Index scale and the duty to provide temperature and humidity devices are as printed by ILO. The ministry's own guide and the decree text were not fetched.

The Qatar, plantation and Singapore results are ILO summaries. The underlying Qatar Red Crescent counts, the programme studies and the Singapore pilot paper were not fetched, so exact counts are not available.

No lightning lead time study specific to strikes on workers, or to the Gulf, was found. The lead times come from severe-weather warning studies (US, Beijing) and a single-station model whose region and hit rates are not in the abstract. The publisher page for that model is behind a cookie redirect.

No numeric evidence was found that forecast-based scheduling beats a fixed schedule on productivity. The closest numbers are the plantation programme (productivity up 10 to 20 percent) and the one-day Singapore pilot (10 percent more steps).
The wearable evidence is a model validation (core temperature from heart rate). It is not a trial showing fewer heat illnesses.

Publisher pages at AMS, Wiley, Nature, Springer, PubMed, the Federal Register, and the WMO and WHO libraries blocked WebFetch (403 errors, cookie redirects or script-only pages). Abstracts were taken from Crossref, Europe PMC and Semantic Scholar records, and report text from saved PDFs.

The lives-saved numbers for Ahmedabad, Philadelphia and France are model or before-and-after estimates, not trials. The Ahmedabad range is wide. Philadelphia's lives saved could be 20% to 50% lower after removing deaths that were only brought forward. France's gap is shared between the warning system and other measures.

Verified in this pass but left out because the heat-at-work slice already holds them: ILO 2024 exposure and death counts (2.41 billion workers, 18,970 deaths a year, 83.6% of Arab States workers), the Saudi 2026 midday ban results (29,945 inspections, 95% compliance, 1,771 violations) and the OSHA 2024 proposed rule (531 deaths and 16,027 injuries prevented a year, US$7.8 billion a year cost).
Every figure here is an external published result. None measures what a WakeCap system or its data bank achieves.
